opus-5.5.text:
I think reading groups are one of the quieter but more important parts of how we work. Robotics and AI move so fast now that no single person can keep up with everything: new vision-language models, new training recipes, new hardware, new datasets. A reading group spreads that load. Someone goes deep on a paper, comes back, and in an hour the whole group gets the core idea, plus that person's honest take on whether it actually matters.

What I value most isn't the summary, though. It's the discussion. People from very different backgrounds sit in the same room: people who've spent years on low-level control, people from large-scale language modeling, people who mostly think about data and infrastructure. They read the same paper and react completely differently. The controls person says, "This won't hold up on real hardware because of X," and the ML person says, "But if you scale the data, maybe X goes away." Those disagreements are where a lot of our research directions actually start.

It also shapes culture. It sets a norm that it's fine to say "I don't understand this," or "I think this result is overstated," even if the paper comes from a famous lab, or from us. Being critical but curious about the literature carries over into how we look at our own experiments.

And it connects to how we share ideas outward. A lot of what we eventually write up or talk about publicly was first tested informally in those conversations: does this framing make sense, is this the real contribution, what would a skeptic say? So in a way, the reading group is a rehearsal space for the ideas we put into the world.

For a young field like general-purpose robot learning, where nobody really knows the right recipe yet, that kind of shared, ongoing thinking is pretty essential. It keeps us from getting too attached to one approach too early.

r002.rationale: It says ideas may be tested informally in conversations, but does not describe bringing a nearly mature project back to the group for feedback.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe an internal user demonstrating a new tool or sharing practical knowledge of how to use it.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly, with no tools.

Reading groups are honestly one of the things I'd point to if you asked me what makes PI feel different from other places I've worked. Robotics right now sits at the intersection of so many fields. You have people coming from language modeling, from diffusion and video generation, from classical control, from hardware, and nobody has the full picture. The reading group is where those pictures collide.

The way it works in practice is pretty informal. Someone flags a paper, sometimes something brand new, sometimes something old that suddenly feels relevant again, and we spend an hour pulling it apart. The interesting part is almost never the paper itself. It's the moment when someone from the data side says "we actually see the opposite of that in our teleop logs," or someone from the model side says "we tried this six months ago and here's why it didn't transfer." That's where a lot of our actual research directions get born. You get a very fast feedback loop between what the community is publishing and what we're seeing on real robots, which are two things that don't always agree.

It also does something more subtle, which is that it keeps us honest about ideas we didn't come up with. It's easy in a lab with a strong thesis to only read work that confirms the thesis. Having a regular slot where someone presents a paper that argues the other way is a kind of immune system for groupthink.

And on the sharing side, it sets the tone for how we talk about our own work. If you've been in a room where your colleagues have spent an hour poking holes in someone else's paper, you write your own papers and blog posts differently. You anticipate the questions. You show the failure cases. I think a lot of why we try to release things with real detail, the data mixtures, the things that didn't work, comes from that culture of reading critically together. You start to see openness less as a marketing choice and more as the natural extension of how the group already thinks.

astra-6.text:
I think reading groups can create a shared language. People come to Physical Intelligence with different backgrounds and different intuitions, and discussing a paper gives them something concrete to reason about together. What is the central idea? What evidence supports it? What would it mean for the problems we’re working on?

The most useful part is often the disagreement. Someone sees a promising direction; someone else notices an assumption that might break when you put it on a robot. Working through that helps turn an individual insight into something the team can understand, challenge, and build on.

People come in with different backgrounds and different intuitions, and discussing a paper together gives them a chance to understand how other people think. The useful part isn’t just summarizing the result; it’s asking, “What do we believe here? What would we try differently? How does this connect to the problems we’re working on?” That can turn reading into a starting point for new ideas, and it makes those ideas easier to share across the team.
